claims.text: An ML model incorporating experimentally quantified defects, 1 wt.% oxygen, and associated lattice distortions will predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than conventional analytical models.
In the 0–200 K regime, oxygen contamination and defects will substantially suppress conductivity through impurity scattering and carrier localization.
In the 300–1200 K regime, thermal activation will overcome defect-induced localization and produce a moderate conductivity increase.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr has natural lattice distortions relevant to its electrical transport.
The modeled and tested specimen will contain 1 wt.% oxygen.
The predictive model will be trained using experimental measurements and ab initio calculations that encompass defect structures and oxygen effects.
Defect and impurity scattering dominate electrical transport in HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 200 K.
Thermally activated transport processes are prevalent in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen-induced defects and lattice distortions alter the local electronic structure of the alloy.
Oxygen-induced defects and lattice distortions alter carrier-scattering rates in the alloy.
At low temperature, oxygen-related defects increase scattering and create localized electronic states that reduce conductivity.
At high temperature, phonon activation partially delocalizes carriers and counteracts defect effects.
Representing defect scattering and thermal activation will allow the ML model to resolve their nonlinear temperature-dependent interplay more accurately than perfect-crystal approaches.
The ML model will predict lower conductivity from 0 to 200 K than perfect-crystal models.
From 300 to 1200 K, the ML predictions will show a smooth thermally activated conductivity increase that closely matches measurements.
The ML model will reduce prediction error by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional analytical predictions.
Conventional defect-free analytical models typically overestimate low-temperature conductivity and mischaracterize high-temperature conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The stated applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen between 0 and 1200 K.
Failure to improve accuracy by at least 10–20% over conventional models is a falsifying result.
